cards.title: Patrick Stewart has died

cards.title: DoorDash to acquire Instacart

depth.text: DoorDash plans to **buy Instacart**, saying the deal could help **local stores** reach more customers

The agreement values Instacart at **$65.00 per share**, or approximately **$17 billion** in equity; at least 75% of the payment would be cash. Instacart customers could shop at more than **50,000 additional stores**, while DashPass and Instacart+ members would pay one fee instead of two.

cards.camps: Two camps: some worry about antitrust and delivery workers; others think the deal could help compete with Walmart and Amazon.

cards.title: Google Search is now less than half of Alphabet’s revenue

depth.text: Google Search is now **under half** of Alphabet’s revenue, while its own revenue still grew

Search brought in **$63.4B** of Alphabet’s $128B in the quarter to Sep 2026, or **49.7%**—the first quarter below half since Alphabet began reporting Search revenue separately. Search revenue still grew 12% year over year; Google Cloud grew **103%**, and the share fell because the rest of Alphabet grew faster.

cards.camps: Two camps: some call the lower Search share healthy diversification; others think Google's AI push is weakening Search.

comments.text: I get what they're trying to say, but it still seems a bit unconventional to have a line chart where the y-axis is a share percentage. Here's a graph with revenue in dollars by segment: https://www.pasteboard.co/DwvXdQj2LXpk.png

cards.title: LLM Voice

The author says even human edits may not remove **LLM-Voice**, and thinks LLMs may help with **outlines**, but writers should supply the prose. They make an exception for **Jim Highsmith**, who finds an LLM essential to his writing because of Parkinson's disease.

cards.camps: Two camps: some find LLM prose tiring, repetitive, or soulless; others say AI helps people with writing difficulties share ideas and see blanket dismissal as privilege.

cards.title: H.264 Is Magic (2016)

depth.text: someone breaks down how **video compression** throws away detail and reuses frames to make files **tiny**
Using an Apple homepage clip, the article explains **quantization**, **chroma subsampling** and motion compensation. It says its 300-frame video stores only **three actual frames**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say they keep sharing or rereading it; one commenter says its quantization explanation could leave beginners with the wrong idea.

comments.text: Had the pleasure of working with Jason Garrett-Glaser (better known as DarkShikari) circa 2011 on a patch for x264 to better utilize more cores (slice-threaded lookahead). At the time he was working with Sony to optimize their PlayStation game streaming service, and this had the potential to lower encoding latency (critical to game streaming) even on same-core systems by spreading the frame over…

One uncommonly used feature of H.264 is support for lossless video. It's a bit hard to use due to tooling (not easy to discover and select the feature), and is sometimes incompatible with web browsers, but you can get actual lossless video using a mainstream video codec. You can verify that it really is lossless, and doesn't have any conversion step where it's quantized to 8-bit YUV. "x264vfw" is…
Ten years later, 2026 magic: AV1 https://engineering.fb.com/2026/06/22/video-engineering/adop... And soon AV2 https://av2.aomedia.org/

Previous discussions: 4.nov.2016 https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=12871403 219 comments 17.mar.2022 https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=30710574 219 comments 24.may.2019 https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19997813 180 comments 14.jun.2024 https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40681306 205 comments

Hutter prize (I think mentioned in a 3b1b video somewhere else in this thread) is a great example. Given this…

cards.title: The US added a record 20.2 GWh of battery storage in just 3 months

depth.text: the US added a **record amount** of **battery storage** in one quarter, mostly for the grid

Arizona alone added a record **6.2 GWh**, the strongest quarter ever recorded by a single state, while residential installations fell **27%** year over year. Benchmark raised its storage forecast through 2030 by 11.5%, to 683 GWh.

cards.camps: Some commenters emphasize batteries’ role in smoothing demand spikes and helping stabilize the grid; others say the added storage covers only a short slice of peak demand and that much more is needed.

cards.title: Forging a Microsoft Edge Full Chain with Logic Bugs Only

Orange Tsai turned a **navigation flaw** into a **UXSS**, then used Immersive Reader’s file-write bug to overwrite protocols.json. He paired that file with a tiny executable to get **code execution**.

comments.text: Orange is a legend and this chain is extremely impressive here. No memory corruptions, no heap shenanigans, just pure logic bugs, almost made easy to understand for the reader. I always felt bad about the whole site/browser cross integration that chrome and edge and others do. Now I feel really really really bad about it. cards.title: If IPv4 were land

depth.text: someone redrew the world map so **country sizes** reflect their share of **internet addresses**

The formula scales each country's share of world IPv4 addresses by total land area; land area comes from **map geometry, not official figures**. **About 70 small territories** with no outline at that resolution are left out, accounting for around 52M addresses, mostly Hong Kong, Singapore and Mauritius. Counts come from IP Trust's geolocation database, October 2026.

comments.text: India: 47M China: 358M Both countries have roughly the same population. The IPv4 problem has been swept under the rug with CGNAT and a normal person doesn't even notice it. But it sucks. Forget having a dedicated IP, even on a broadband connection, you don't get a public IP that's truly yours. According to IPInfo[1], there are around 1,000 users sharing my IP. I get flagged for malicious…

From a Georgist perspective, IPv4 is actually a form of land (it's a finite "natural resource", although that's not quite proper), and you could make a case for "land rent" being taxed on the addresses. This is the same as radio broadcast frequencies, web addresses, actual land, un-mined gold/oil/coal/whatever, and other finite natural resources that create monopolistic tendencies.

The only thing that surprised me was that Canada was so small compared to other Western countries. But I suppose that might be an artifact. The map shows IPv4 proportional to land area, but a "fair" allocation would have IPv4 proportionate to population, not land area, and I'd assume Canada is (overall) less densely populated than most other developed countries.
IPv6 got some real traction in the last decade. From around 10% adoption up to 50%. It's not dead, like many are claiming. It works fine, just keep implementing it.
at a certain point in time there has to be a forcing function or event that causes people to migrate from ipv4 to ipv6.

cards.title: How Google determines the names for bodies of water in Google Earth (2008)

Its rule counted names in **widespread daily use**, rather than accepting **arbitrary government renamings** automatically. For disputed waters, Google said it would show **both names**, with labels nearer the countries that use them.

cards.camps: Critics said Google applied its own rules inconsistently to the Persian Gulf naming dispute; others argued maps should follow official sources or local-language preferences.

comments.text: "By saying "common", we mean to include names which are in widespread daily use, rather than giving immediate recognition to any arbitrary governmental re-naming. In other words, if a ruler announced that henceforth the Pacific Ocean would be named after her mother, we would not add that placemark unless and until the name came into common usage. " They violated their own policy with the gulf…

Disclaimer: work for Google This article is not as pure as it might seem but I think this is also a post-hoc reasoning to explain what decision they went with for the "Persian Gulf" / "Arabian Gulf" decision, and Google then proceeded to change their stance on that in the following years: "Google had previously put both Persian Gulf and Arabian Gulf on its Google Maps. After May 2012, it removed…

The key quote: > But if different countries dispute the proper name for a body of water, our policy is to display both names, with each label placed closer to the country or countries that use it. Clearly that policy has changed since 2008. Not surprising, since that's before they decided to officially be evil.

cards.title: Tomáš Mikolov awarded the Medal of Merit by the President of the Czech Republic

depth.text: Tomáš Mikolov received the **Medal of Merit** for his work in **science**

He is best known as one of the creators of **Word2Vec**, which represents words as **mathematical vectors** to capture relationships between their meanings. The article says this approach became one of the important foundations for modern **language models**.

comments.text: Deserved. word2vec is a beautiful peice of science. The hypothesis behind it was so amazing. I kinda feel like everything else in LLMs (including the attention mechanism itself) is just engineering around the representation learning breakthrough that word2vec demonstrated
I remember being presented Word2Vec as an undergrad in 2016 and I could not predict the sci-fi reality that is today

Well-deserved. glossary.TNG: Star Trek: The Next Generation: the Star Trek show that featured Captain Picard.
glossary.open-weight: Describes an AI whose learned settings are available for others to download and use.
glossary.reinforcement learning: A way to train an AI by rewarding choices that work and discouraging choices that do not.
glossary.tokens: Small pieces of text an AI counts as it reads or writes; they can affect how much a request costs.
glossary.FBI: Federal Bureau of Investigation: a US agency that investigates federal crimes.
glossary.wiretap: Secretly listening to or recording someone's phone calls or conversations.
glossary.equity value: The value assigned to all a company's shares in the deal.
glossary.proration: When too many shareholders choose the same kind of payment, each person's share of it is reduced.
glossary.antitrust: Rules meant to stop companies from becoming so powerful that they can squeeze out competition.
glossary.year over year: A way to compare a figure with the same period one year earlier.
glossary.moat: An advantage that makes it hard for competitors to take customers away from a business.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.hallucination: When an AI gives made-up or incorrect information as if it were true.
glossary.agentic: Describes AI that chooses steps and acts toward a task, rather than only answering a question.
glossary.SAFU: Secure Asset Fund for Users: Binance's fund set aside to help cover losses.
glossary.CEX: Centralized exchange: a company-run place where people trade crypto and the company holds their funds.
glossary.stablecoin: A kind of crypto designed to keep its price steady, often by being linked to regular money.
glossary.fiat money: Money issued by a government, such as dollars, rather than a crypto coin.
glossary.wallet: A tool for keeping the secret information needed to access and send crypto.
glossary.BTC: Bitcoin: a type of digital money.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.LLM-Voice: A writing style that readers feel sounds like text produced by an AI.
glossary.uncanny valley: The uneasy feeling people get when something looks or sounds almost human, but not quite.
glossary.stylometry: The study of writing patterns, which can help compare or identify different writers.
glossary.codec: A set of rules that shrinks video for storage or sending and turns it back into a playable picture.
glossary.lossy compression: Shrinking a file by permanently dropping some details.
glossary.lossless compression: Making an image file smaller without losing any of the original image information.
glossary.quantization: A way to make a model use less computing power by representing its internal numbers less precisely.
glossary.chroma subsampling: Keeping less color detail than brightness detail, since people notice fine brightness changes more easily.
glossary.motion compensation: Saving how parts of one frame shift between frames instead of saving every frame as a new full picture.
glossary.I-frame: A complete video frame that can be decoded without relying on earlier frames.
glossary.P-frame: A frame described using movement from an earlier frame.
glossary.B-frame: A frame that uses both earlier and later frames to work out its picture.
glossary.macro-block: A square chunk of a frame that the codec tracks for movement.
glossary.motion vector: A direction-and-distance note for how one block shifts between frames.
glossary.entropy encoder: A step that replaces repeated patterns with a shorter description, without losing information.
glossary.EV: Electric vehicle: a car that runs on electricity instead of petrol or diesel.
glossary.e-waste: Discarded electronics that are no longer useful and may create waste problems.
glossary.GWh: Gigawatt-hours: a measure of an amount of electricity, often used to describe how much a battery can store.
glossary.utility-scale: Large enough to serve the shared electricity grid, rather than just one home or business.
glossary.standalone storage: Battery storage installed without a solar project paired with it.
glossary.virtual power plant: A group of smaller energy sources, like home batteries, coordinated to act like one power source.
glossary.demand-response: Programs that ask customers to use less electricity or shift when they use it to help the grid.
glossary.PHP2Shell: The name used here for the PHP vulnerability attackers tried to exploit.
glossary.Fragnesia: The name of a Linux flaw that lets an attacker move from limited access to full control of a computer.
glossary.root: The highest level of control on a computer, with permission to change system settings and files.
glossary.Active Directory: A system organizations use to manage accounts, groups, and access to their computers.
glossary.webshell: A script on a web server that lets someone send it commands from elsewhere.
glossary.reverse SSH tunnel: A connection started from a compromised computer back to an attacker, opening a route into the network behind it.
glossary.PAN-OS: The software that runs on the affected Palo Alto Networks firewalls.
glossary.PHP: PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor; a language people use to make websites work.
glossary.single sign-on: A way to sign in to a service using an account you already have with another service.
glossary.hacktivist: A hacker who breaks into systems or exposes data to make a political point.
glossary.doxing: Finding and publishing someone’s private details without permission.
glossary.freedom of information request: A request asking a government agency to release records it holds.
glossary.chain of command: The line showing who reports to whom in an organization.
glossary.espionage: Secretly gathering information someone has kept confidential, without their permission.
glossary.proprietary information: Information a company keeps private rather than making public.
glossary.classified information: Information a government has marked as secret and limits who can see.
glossary.honeypot: A computer set up to attract attacks so people can watch what attackers do.
glossary.export restrictions: Government rules that limit what can be sold or sent to other countries.
glossary.open weight: An AI model whose learned settings are available for people to download and use.
glossary.self-hostable: Able to run on computers you control, instead of only through a company's service.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.UXSS: Universal Cross-Site Scripting: a flaw that lets code from one website run as if it came from another website.
glossary.ACE: Arbitrary Code Execution: a security flaw that lets someone make a computer run instructions they choose.
glossary.PE: Portable Executable: the kind of file Windows uses for a program it can run.
glossary.IPv4: Internet Protocol version 4: a system for giving devices numerical addresses so data can reach them online.
glossary.IPv6: Internet Protocol version 6: a newer system for online addresses, with room for far more of them.
glossary.CGNAT: Carrier-Grade Network Address Translation: lets an internet provider have many customers share one public address.
glossary.geolocation database: A collection of records that estimates where internet addresses are located.
glossary.placemark: A marker placed on a map to identify a spot.
glossary.geolocation: Figuring out where a signal came from.
glossary.post-hoc reasoning: An explanation made after a decision has already been made.
glossary.Word2Vec: A method for turning words into numbers in a way that captures how their meanings relate.
glossary.mathematical vector: A list of numbers used to represent something so a computer can compare it with other things.
glossary.language model: Software that learns patterns in language and can work with text.
glossary.attention mechanism: A way for a text program to focus on the parts that matter as it processes language.
glossary.Emacs: A text editor with many ways to move around and change text.
glossary.Emacs-like: An editor that borrows the feel or commands of Emacs.
glossary.syntax highlighting: Coloring parts of code to make them easier to recognize.
glossary.multi-buffer: Keeping several pieces of text open so you can switch between them.
glossary.splits: Showing more than one text area on screen at once.
glossary.floor division: Division that rounds down toward negative infinity, rather than toward zero.
glossary.compile-time constant: A value fixed before a program runs, so the compiler can use it when preparing the code.
glossary.throughput: How many operations a computer can finish over a stretch of time.
glossary.latency: The time between doing something and seeing the device respond.
glossary.SIMD: Single Instruction, Multiple Data: a way to apply one operation to several values at once.
glossary.CPU cache: A small, fast storage area in a processor that keeps data handy so it can be used quickly.
glossary.side channel: A clue you can learn from a device's normal behavior, even when it is not directly sharing that information.
glossary.air gap: A setup where a computer or network has no connection to outside networks.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.CI configuration: Continuous integration configuration: instructions that tell a system what checks or tasks to run when code changes.
glossary.regular expression: A text pattern that tells a program what kind of words or characters to look for.
glossary.container image: A ready-made bundle of an app and the files it needs to run on a server.
glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.SMS: Short Message Service: text messages sent between phones.
glossary.WAP Push: A kind of mobile message that can deliver information directly to a phone.
glossary.zero-click: A way to get software onto a device without the person tapping a link or opening a file.
glossary.DoS: Denial of Service: an attack that makes a computer or service stop working for its users.
glossary.uintvar: A way to store a number in a message using a variable number of bytes.
glossary.NegativeArraySizeException: An error raised when a program tries to make an array with a negative size.
glossary.SQLite: A small database that can be stored in a single file.
glossary.ADB: Android Debug Bridge: a tool for sending commands from a computer to an Android device.
glossary.eSIM: Embedded SIM: a SIM built into a device instead of a removable card.
glossary.FEC: Federal Election Commission: a US agency the article points to for official election information.
glossary.VPN: Virtual private network: a service that sends your internet traffic through another computer, often to protect it or make it appear to come from somewhere else.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.OpenGL ES: A set of tools for drawing graphics, designed for devices with more limited hardware.
glossary.WebGL 2: A browser-based way for websites to draw interactive 3D graphics.
glossary.WebGPU: A browser feature that lets a web page run calculations on your device’s graphics chip.
glossary.Vulkan: A way for software to send graphics work to a graphics card.
glossary.state machine: A system that remembers its current settings, so later commands can behave differently depending on earlier ones.
glossary.rasterizer: Software that turns drawn shapes into colored dots on a screen.
glossary.ray tracer: A program that makes images by working out how light would bounce around a scene.
glossary.GLSL: OpenGL Shading Language: a language used to write instructions for how graphics should look.
glossary.canvas fingerprinting: Drawing something on a webpage’s canvas and using tiny differences in how it looks to recognize a browser setup.
glossary.obfuscation: Making something harder to see or recognize.
glossary.Node: Software that lets JavaScript run outside a web browser.
glossary.jailbreak prompt: Text meant to trick an AI into ignoring its usual rules.
glossary.RISC-V: A processor design that sets out the basic instructions software runs on.
glossary.Gated DeltaNet: A kind of model layer that can keep information in a changing internal memory.
glossary.RAM: Random-Access Memory: a computer's working space for information it is using right now.
glossary.forward pass: One run through a model to produce an answer, rather than building it one piece at a time.
glossary.one-hot key: A way to point at one memory slot by marking just that slot in a list.
glossary.free-running: A test run where the CPU keeps going on its own, without another machine correcting each step.
glossary.local maxima: High points on a graph compared with nearby points.
glossary.LLMs: Large language models: computer programs trained on lots of writing that can produce text.
glossary.Bun: A program that lets JavaScript run outside a web browser.
glossary.preload: A file a program loads before its normal work starts, often to add or change behavior.
glossary.token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
glossary.cache hit: When software finds saved information it needs and can reuse it.
glossary.OpenTelemetry: A way to collect and send records about what software is doing, such as its requests.
glossary.subagent: A helper assigned a smaller part of a larger task.
glossary.rate-limit headroom: How much usage room remains before a service restricts you for using too much.
glossary.agent_summary: The label the article uses for background-agent summary requests in its usage records.
glossary.chemotherapy: Medicine used to kill cancer cells, though it can also affect healthy parts of the body.
glossary.lumbar puncture: A procedure where a needle goes into the lower back to take or replace fluid around the spine.
glossary.lymphoma: A cancer that starts in the body's infection-fighting system.
glossary.port catheter: A small device under the skin that connects to a blood vessel so medicine can go in.
glossary.LTS: Long-term support: a release its makers promise to support for an extended period.
glossary.atrial fibrillation: A heart rhythm problem that can make the heartbeat uneven.
glossary.immunotherapy: Treatment that helps the body's immune system fight cancer.
glossary.certificate: A digital ID that helps show which website a connection belongs to.
glossary.TLS: Transport Layer Security: a way to scramble information as it travels between devices, so others can’t read it.
glossary.intermediate CA: Certificate authority: a service trusted to confirm website identities; an intermediate one is a middle link that can vouch for a website's certificate.
glossary.root CA: Certification Authority: the top-level organization a device trusts when deciding whether a website's certificate is valid.
glossary./etc/ssl/cert.pem: A Mac file some command-line tools use as their list of trusted certificate issuers.
glossary.resin printer: A 3D printer that hardens liquid resin with light to build a part layer by layer.
glossary.MSLA: Masked Stereolithography: a resin-printing method that uses a screen to shine light on selected areas and harden a layer.
glossary.FDM: Fused Deposition Modeling: a 3D printer builds an object by laying down melted plastic in thin lines.
glossary.VOC: Volatile organic compounds: Gases that can come from products and materials and affect indoor air.
glossary.Open Material Mode: A setting that lets the printer use materials made by other companies, not just Formlabs.
glossary.UL GREENGUARD Gold: A certification for products tested for low chemical emissions.
glossary.IPA: Isopropyl alcohol: a solvent used here to wash leftover resin off prints.
